notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0267c.stoa003.opp-l: Bracketed source references (Leo, Gregory, Theodosian Code, Hadrianic collection, etc.) are the editor's marginal citations printed in the text and are kept; page numbers (999–1001) and footnote marks are omitted. In the Ecclesiasticus passage, 'ad carnem' is read as 'ad canem' (dog), as in the Vulgate of Ecclus. 13:22; 'Iconis' read as 'leonis', 'dicitum' as 'divitum', 'de ede' as 'de pede', 'humilia' as 'humilis', 'factat' as 'faciat'. 'Qui curiae deserviunt' probably means those bound to service on a municipal council (curiales).

Line 1: the consular date is the edition's; the bracketed years are as printed. Summary: 'admiiti' read as 'admitti'. Ch. IV: 'Nullus anathema' read with the canon rubric as 'nullus anathematizatus'; 'infainis' read as 'infamis'. Ch. V: 'Per scripti' read as 'per scripta'; 'co' as 'eo'; the Hincmar reference 'lib. LV]' is garbled as printed. Ch. VIII: 'inter provinciam' taken as 'intra provinciam'; 'rei adversus quamcunque professio' taken as the declaration of a defendant (reus). 'Familiares' (members of the household, or close associates) is ambiguous.

Line 4: the clause 'sic odit Deus eos qui adversus patrum invasores, qui in mundo patres armantur, ut infamia sunt notati' is garbled in the edition; translated on the likely sense 'those who arm themselves against the fathers'. The closing 'Creator omnium populorum, Creator omnium' is a printing dittography and is rendered once. Obvious scanning errors (faerimus, von, tames, qnoniam, cos, maltum, injunctura, pervenian, etc.) silently corrected. The reference '1 Cor. 15' for 'ut sermo Dei currat' is as printed; the quotation is from 2 Thess. 3:1. 'Excutite pulverem... in testimonium illis' rendered 'against them' following the sense of the Gospel passage.

nodes.text: APPENDIX. DECRETAL LETTERS ATTRIBUTED TO ST STEPHEN.
(I) LETTER I.
TO BISHOP HILARIUS.

SUMMARY.— Who are infamous, and who are not to be admitted to ecclesiastical grades or to bringing accusations. On the reverence to be shown to superiors, and on the vestments of ministers, that they should be consecrated.
TO HIS MOST BELOVED BROTHER AND INTIMATE FRIEND HILARIUS, BISHOP STEPHEN [SENDS] GREETING OF HEARTFELT CHARITY.

Although I hope (St Leo, letter 46) that your Love is devoted to every good work, nevertheless, on account of the close friendship by which you are known to be joined to us, and so that your diligence may become more effective, it has seemed fitting to us that we should send this brotherly letter to your Love. We admonish you, dearest brother, always to remain in good things and to beware of evil; to be constantly with good men, of right faith and holy manner of life, and to keep apart from the perverse and from those who lay snares for the brethren, unless it is to convert them and bring them back to concord; since, as the Apostle says, evil conversations corrupt good morals (1 Cor. 15). And the Truth himself says: If your eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and throw it from you. And if your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it from you. Likewise one must act concerning the foot, because it is better for you to enter the kingdom of heaven one-eyed or lame than, having two eyes or two hands or two feet, to be sent into the Gehenna of fire (Matt. 18; Mark 9). And in the book Ecclesiasticus it is found: In a man's good fortune his enemies [are friendly]; but in his sorrow and his trouble a friend is recognised. An enemy speaks sweetly with his lips, but in his heart he lies in wait to overthrow you into a pit. And: He who touches pitch will be defiled by it. And: He who associates with a proud man will put on pride. He takes a burden upon himself who associates with one more honourable than himself. Do not be the companion of one richer than you. What fellowship will the kettle have with the earthen pot? When they strike together, it will be broken. The rich man will do wrong and will bluster, but the poor man, when injured, will keep silent. If you are generous, he will take you up; and if you have nothing, he will abandon you. If you have [means], he will live with you and will empty you, and he himself will not grieve over you; if you are useful to him, he will trip you up, and smiling he will give you hope, telling you fine things, and he will say: What do you need? And he will put you to shame with his dinners, until he has drained you twice and three times; and in the end he will laugh at you. Afterwards, seeing [you], he will abandon you, and will shake his head at you. Humble yourself to God and wait for his hands. Take care that you are not led astray and humbled in folly. Do not be humble in your wisdom, lest, being humbled, you be led astray into folly. When invited by one more powerful, withdraw: for by this he will invite you all the more. Do not be forward, lest you be thrust back; and do not stand far off from him, lest you pass into oblivion. Do not presume to speak with him as an equal, and do not believe his many words. For with much talk he will test you, and smiling he will question you about your secrets. His cruel mind will store up your words, and he will not spare you harm or chains. Beware for yourself, and pay careful attention to what you hear, since you walk along with your own overthrow. Hearing these things as if in sleep, look, and you will be awake. All your life love God, and call upon him for your salvation. Every animal loves its like, and so every man [loves] his neighbour. All flesh joins itself to its like, and every man associates with one like himself. If the wolf ever has fellowship with the lamb, so [will] the sinner with the righteous. What fellowship has a holy man with a dog? Or what good peace has the rich man with the poor? The wild ass in the desert is the lion's prey; so the poor are the pasture of the rich. And as humility is an abomination to the proud, so the poor man is an abhorrence to the rich. The rich man, when shaken, is held up by his friends; but the humble man, when he falls, will be driven away even by his acquaintances. When a rich man is deceived, many come to his rescue; he has spoken proud things, and they have justified him: the humble man is deceived, and on top of that he is rebuked. He has spoken sensibly, and no place was given him. The rich man has spoken, and all were silent, and they will carry his word up to the clouds. The poor man has spoken, and they say: Who is this? And if he stumbles, they will overthrow him. Wealth is good to him who has no sin on his conscience, and poverty is most wicked in the mouth of the ungodly. A man's heart changes his face, whether for good or for evil. The mark of a good heart and a good face you will find with difficulty, and with toil (Ecclus. 12, 13). Of this, brother, beware for yourself, and do not go after your desires (Ecclus. 23:30).

I. As to your consulting the apostolic See about who are infamous, or who are not to be admitted to ecclesiastical grades, we believe that you know this, and yet we do not refuse to instruct you by the authority of the apostolic See. We say, then, that those persons are infamous who are branded with infamy for some fault (C. 6 q. 1; and in Ivo's Decretum, book 4), that is, all who cast off the rule of the Christian law and despise the ecclesiastical statutes; likewise thieves, the sacrilegious, and all entangled in capital crimes; also violators of tombs, and those who wilfully violate the statutes of the apostles and their successors and of the other Fathers, and all who take up arms against the Fathers (Anianus on the Sentences of Paul, book 1, tit. 2; const. 2, tit. 39, Theodosian Code), who are branded with infamy throughout the whole world. Likewise the incestuous, murderers, perjurers, abductors (Proclus to Domnus; Hadrianic collection, ch. 17), sorcerers, poisoners, adulterers, deserters from wars, and those who seek to hold positions unworthy of them, or unjustly take away the property of the Church, and those (Anianus on const. 8, tit. 39, book 9, Theodosian Code) who slander or accuse brethren and do not prove [it]; or who provoke the minds of princes to anger against the innocent (Theodosian Code, book 9, tit. 1, ch. 11; Hadrianic collection 48); and all who are anathematised, or driven from the Church for their crimes, and all whom the ecclesiastical (Anianus, const. 3, tit. 39, book 9, Theodosian Code) or secular laws declare infamous. These it is not permitted (Hadrianic collection 119) to promote to sacred orders, nor slaves before lawful freedom, nor penitents, nor bigamists, nor those who serve the curia, or who are not whole in body, or do not have a sound mind or understanding, or are disobedient to the decrees of the saints, or are manifestly mad: none of these ought to be advanced to sacred grades; nor can these, nor freedmen, nor suspected persons, nor those who do not have the right faith or a worthy manner of life, accuse the chief bishops.

II. But how obedience (St Gregory, letter 10, book 4) or reverence is to be shown to superiors, you yourself are in no doubt, from your own subjects as well. In this matter it is very useful if praiseworthy humility observes, with no one compelling it, what the rigour of discipline imposes (the same, letter 34 of the same book). May almighty God, in whose hand are all things, of whom it is written: There is no wisdom, there is no counsel against the Lord (Prov. 28), himself grant that you and yours keep unimpaired both the divine institutions and those of the apostolic See, and that we and all the faithful may always ascend to better things, and from day to day avoid worse things, and pursue and accomplish what is better and pleasing to God.

III. Ecclesiastical vestments, in which the Lord is served and divine worship is celebrated with all honour and propriety by the priests and the other ministers of the Church, must be both consecrated and seemly. Since they have been consecrated and dedicated to God and his service, no one ought to use them for other purposes than ecclesiastical offices worthy of God. Nor ought they to be touched or carried by others than consecrated men, lest the divine vengeance that struck King Belshazzar come upon those who transgress in these things and presume such acts, and the just scourge of divine vengeance cause them to fall to the depths. Make these things known to all in the parts where you dwell, and in all places you can, and order them to be observed by apostolic authority; for our own people too, and those entrusted to us in the holy apostolic and universal Church, have all professed to observe these things, now and in times to come. With these words, brother, I have briefly and generously answered your letter. May your Love so join itself to them that nothing in what pertains to the state of the universal Church is done either doubtfully or sluggishly (St Leo, letter 46). And let all things be done with such moderation that neither the claims of kindness nor those of justice are neglected, but that, without respect of persons, the judgement of God is kept in mind in all things. That this may be kept with right observance, let the integrity of the catholic faith first be preserved. And since the way that leads to life is in every respect narrow and strait, let there be no turning aside from its path either to the left or to the right.
Given on the fifth day before the Nones of May, in the consulship of Valerian and Gallicanus, men of most distinguished rank (years 254, 255 and 257).
LETTER II.

SUMMARY.—On the expulsion of bishops, and that whatever is done unjustly against things consecrated to God and against bishops is to be reckoned as sacrilege; and that no one's accusation is to be received in writing; and on many other useful matters. On the accusations of priests. II. On bishops despoiled of their property, or driven from their see. III. If anyone presumes to accuse bishops, or agents or defenders of the Church, before he meets with them in charity, that he is to be punished. IV. Who ought not to be admitted to make an accusation. V. That an accusation is not to be received in writing, and that no one absent can be accused or accuse, nor ought [anyone to be accused] before he receives an opportunity to defend [himself]. VI. On primates and metropolitans, and on the business of bishops that is to be referred to them. VII. That an accused bishop is to be heard by all the bishops of the province. VIII. That every accusation is to be concluded within the province, unless an appeal has been made to the apostolic See; and on accusations by those implicated in crimes, or who have confessed of their own accord, or who were formerly enemies. IX. If a cleric accuses his bishop, or lays a plot [against him]. X. Whether laymen ought to administer church property. XI. On the persons of accusers. XII. On charges against teachers, and that those condemned by the divine words cannot accuse bishops or testify against them.
STEPHEN, BISHOP OF THE HOLY APOSTOLIC AND UNIVERSAL ROMAN CHURCH, TO ALL THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT THE VARIOUS PROVINCES, GREETING IN THE LORD.

We rejoice greatly in the Lord (St Leo, letter 40), and glory in the gift of his grace, that your faith grows splendidly through good works and spreads most widely; but we are exceedingly afflicted and troubled over your oppression, about which frequent report has been brought to us by brethren travelling to us (the same, letter 87 and following). It ought not to have been that you were shaken by such great oppressions by those by whom you should have been sustained, upheld and honoured. Therefore it is necessary that, the evasions of such men being set aside, by which venomous malice is usually concealed and goodness and truth obscured (the same, letter 35), no small support be given to you by the faithful, and that help be lent by this apostolic See to those whom it is fitting to assist, through divine grace, with the aid of Christ, lest an imprudent purpose advance to the disturbance of the whole Church, and the things that were long ago forbidden by our holy predecessors and the other holy Fathers come to life again. For by consideration of our position (St Gregory, letter 11, book 12) we are compelled not to neglect, for the Lord's sake, the things requiring correction that have come to our notice, but to correct them with fitting amendment. And if secular offices must keep their own order and the discipline handed down by their forebears, who could bear that ecclesiastical orders be thrown into confusion by rash presumption, that what has been heard be neglected, and that what needs correcting be put off, offering no hope?

I. For we have heard that you are accused by certain people, not so much for your own fault as at their pleasure, so that they may seize what is yours; and that you are therefore greatly afflicted and shaken, to such an extent that you are even driven from your own sees, and that on such a pretext your churches and your property are laid waste and plundered. These things, dearest [brethren], ought not to be done, nor repeated again. Yet it is necessary that what is so often usurped be more often restated and forbidden. For whatever is done unjustly against things consecrated to God and against bishops will be reckoned as sacrilege, because they are consecrated and ought not to be violated by anyone.

II. For no bishop (2, q. 2, Nullus episcoporum), while he has been despoiled of his property, or driven from his own see on any pretext, ought to be accused, nor can any charge be brought against him by anyone, before he is fully restored (Roman Councils 3 and 5 under Symmachus; Hadrianic collection); and all things that had been taken from him by any device are to be restored by the laws, and he himself is to be returned according to the rules to his own see and former state, so that the primates and the synod restore completely to the bishop in question all his possessions and everything unjustly taken from him, and all the revenues, before the accusation is taken up; for not only the ecclesiastical laws but also those of the world forbid this to be done.

III. Nor ought any of them, or of the agents or defenders of the churches (Hadrianic collection, ch. 2, from canon 17 of the fifth Council of Orléans), to be accused before any persons until they have first been met in charity two or three times by those who think themselves injured, or who wish to rebuke them for some errors, so that they may receive from them either a private amendment or a just excuse. Whoever presumes [otherwise], let him be kept from the thresholds of the Church until fitting satisfaction [is made].

IV. Accusers (3, q. 5, Accusatores; and above in the decrees of Telesphorus and Julius), moreover, and accusations which the laws of the world do not receive and which our predecessors forbade, we also reject. For let no foreigner become either their accuser or their judge. Hence it is also written of Lot: You came in as a stranger; is it so that you may judge? (Gen. 19). And let no accuser of your people be a slave (Hadrianic collection, various chapters) or a freedman, nor any suspect or infamous person. Let those also be rejected who live with enemies, and all laymen; for attachment of friendship usually stirs up the hostility of slander. Nor are those to be received in an accusation against you who wish to draw you into their own infamy. Let no anathematised person be received (2, q. 2, Nullus anathematizatorum), nor let anyone believe what is said or written by them.

V. I declare also that those are anathematised whom bishops have anathematised by their writings, or whom their statutes anathematise. For let no accuser be received by writing (2, q. 8), but by his own voice, if the person of the accuser is lawful and worthy, namely in the presence of the one whom he wishes to accuse, because no one absent can either be accused or accuse. Yet no man of the aforesaid order can be accused (Hincmar, ch. 15, book 55), nor ought he to answer his accusers, before he has been summoned according to the rules by his primate and receives opportunity for defence and inquiry, to clear away the charges.

VI. For let no metropolitans or other bishops be called primates (the same above in the decrees of Pope Anicetus), except those who hold the first sees (Hadrianic collection 23) and whose cities the ancients determined to be primatial. But the rest, who have obtained the other metropolitan cities, are to be called not primates but either archbishops or metropolitans. For the cities (Dist. 90, Urbes, but under the name of Lucius, not Stephen) and places over which primates ought to preside were established not by moderns but many ages before the coming of Christ, and even the gentiles appealed to their primates in greater matters. In these very cities, after the coming of Christ, the apostles and their successors placed patriarchs or primates, to whom the business of bishops, saving the apostolic authority in all things, and the greater cases are to be referred, after the apostolic See. And although, as the Apostle forbids (1 Cor. 6), accusations ought not to be pursued among Christians, yet if they cannot be prevented, the accusations against bishops ought to be brought by the accusers to the said primates; still, bishops must strive that brethren at odds be constrained to peace rather than to judgement (Fourth Council of Carthage, ch. 26).

VII. A bishop, moreover (Hadrianic collection 25, 27), ought not to be heard or judged otherwise than in the presence of all the bishops of the province, and by all the bishops of the province, for in their absence it neither ought to be nor can be done. Which persons are not to be admitted to accuse them has already been stated in part above, and both these and infamous persons have been listed more fully in the letter which we sent some time ago to Hilarius.

VIII. Let the freedom to accuse not go beyond the bounds of the province, but let every accusation be heard within the province (3, q. 6, Ultra provinciae; and in the decrees of John, book 4) and concluded by the bishops of the province, unless an appeal has been made to the apostolic See alone. And the accused must be denied the freedom to bring charges (3, q. 11, Neganda est; and in the decrees of John, book 4) before they have cleared themselves of the crime by which they are pressed (see Theodosian Code, book 9, const. 10, 11, 12, with Anianus as interpreter; Hadrianic collection); for the confession of those implicated in crimes is not to be believed against others unless they have first proved themselves innocent, since the declaration of a defendant against anyone whatever is dangerous and ought not to be admitted. Members of the household, those who have confessed of their own accord, and those entangled in crimes ought not to be admitted, nor those who (St Ambrose, letter 64) were enemies yesterday, or the day before, or earlier.

IX. Therefore a cleric who has accused his own bishop (3, q. 4, Clericus qui episcopum) or has plotted against him is not to be received, because he has become infamous, and he ought to withdraw from his grade, or be handed over to the *curia* [the municipal council] to serve.

X. To laypeople as well, however devout they may be (the same in the letter of Pope Fabian), we never read that any power was granted of giving answer in any matter concerning church property. We know, most beloved, that the carnal are always wont to persecute the spiritual, and the malicious to defame and tear apart the well-meaning. And therefore the apostles and their successors, and the other holy Fathers, did not want the accusation of bishops to be made easy; for if it were easy, none or scarcely any [bishop] would now be found. For they are called the thrones of God (Eleventh Council of Toledo, ch. 5); therefore they ought not to be shaken, or harassed, or troubled. Of them, then, the Prophet says: The heavens tell the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands (Ps. 18).

XI. Those, however, who are not of good conduct and whose life is open to accusation, or whose faith, life and free status are unknown, cannot accuse them. First, the persons, faith, life and conduct of the accusers must always be examined in detail; and afterwards what they allege is to be faithfully gone into, because nothing ought to be done before the persons, faith, life and conduct of the accusers are carefully examined, lest anyone be harassed through someone's envy or enmity or evil intent (2, q. 7, Quaerendum est; 1, q. 8, Accusatorum personae; and in the decrees of Pope Callistus).

XII. Let no one entertain charges (Hadrianic collection 67) against a teacher, for teachers are to be borne with rather than injured or defamed. Hence the Apostle says: Bear one another's burdens, and so you will fulfil the law of Christ (Gal. 6). Love, moreover, is not ambitious, is not puffed up, does not seek its own things, but those of Jesus Christ (1 Cor. 13). He who abides in love abides in God, and God in him (1 John 4). And he who abides in God wishes to harm no one, but desires to help and sustain all, just as the Lord himself came to save all and to give his life as a ransom for us (Matt. 20). We stop the mouths (Hadrianic collection 29) of those, for accusing priests or testifying against them, whom we recognise to have been condemned by human and divine pronouncements, or to be dead. All, therefore, who persecute the priests of the Lord, whether secretly or openly, must take the utmost care not to be condemned by the commandments of the Lord set out below. Through the prophet Jeremiah the Lord speaks, threatening such people, saying: Your iniquities have turned all things aside, and your sins have removed good things from you, for among my people there are found ungodly men and speakers of vain things; they have set [snares] to destroy men, and have caught them; like a fowler's snare full of birds, so their houses are full of deceit (Jer. 5). And through David he says: Those who have devised evils in their heart have spent all day in battles; they have sharpened their tongues like serpents; the venom of asps is under their lips (Ps. 139). And a little after: Coals of fire shall fall upon them; you will cast them down into pits, so that they do not rise up. A man full of tongue shall not be established on the earth; evils shall seize the unjust man to his ruin. I know that the Lord will maintain the cause of the needy, the judgements of the poor (ibid.). Likewise the same: Let deceitful lips be made dumb (Ps. 19). And again through Micah he says: All are judged in blood; each one afflicts his neighbour; all prepare their hands for evil (Mic. 7, from the Septuagint version). The Lord, foreseeing these men, commanded the apostles that his servants should not easily be torn apart, lest perhaps they be lost or fall into such temptation as they could by no means bear. For this reason the holy apostles and their successors established the rules of the decrees, so that the voice of such men (which strives rather to destroy the innocent and simple than to save them) should not be easily received, but that they themselves should be driven far off by these darts, and should be quite unable to destroy the disciples of the Lord according to their wishes and wiles. Hence the Lord himself also says: Shake the dust off your feet as a testimony against them (Mark 6). And elsewhere the Truth itself speaks of such men in person: It is better for him that a donkey's millstone be hung about his neck and that he be sunk in the depth of the sea than that he should cause one of these little ones to stumble (Matt. 18). And the apostle James says: Judgement without mercy will be [shown] to him who has not shown mercy (James 2). With what face, then, does anyone hope to obtain from God pardon for his sins, who is unwilling to forgive his erring brother anything by way of the duty of kindness and clemency? Surely he must reckon that he will find God in judgement to be such, when he has been set before the tribunal of the just judge, as he showed himself to his brother: For with the measure with which we have measured, it will be measured back to us (Matt. 7). And John, apostle and evangelist, says: He who hates his brother is a murderer. And you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him (1 John 4). You, however, dearest sons, we exhort to bear patiently, with the Lord's support, the evils inflicted on you, and with these apostolic precepts drive such men far off, so that they cannot tear or bite you in the manner of dogs. Remember also that, according to the voice of the Psalmist (St Boniface, letter 26): Man, his days are like grass; like a flower of the field, so will he flourish (Ps. 102). And the apostle says: The whole world lies in the evil one (1 John 5). Hence we pray that you not fear such men much, for they are infamous and cannot harm you much, since their voice has been extinguished; for God so hates those (Proclus to Domnus; Hadrianic collection 71) who take up arms against the fathers, [as] invaders of the fathers in the world, that they are branded with infamy. Arm yourselves, therefore, with these apostolic supports against them, and strengthen your hearts with a guiding spirit, so that God, who willed you to be called shepherds among his people, may not find you negligent or lukewarm, or fleeing when wolves come upon you, but may always find you, after the example of the good shepherd, manfully defending the lambs together with their mothers and the sons and daughters, and faithfully bringing back holy mother Church. And although (St Boniface, letter 25) the days are evil, yet do not be unwise, but understanding what the will of God is (Eph. 5). Therefore be strong, and stand firm in the faith, acting manfully, and let all your deeds be done in love (1 Cor. 16), and, according to the holy Gospel, in your patience you will possess your souls (Luke 12). Remember also the holy apostles and prophets; and because they laboured much in the Lord, they therefore obtained everlasting rewards. Know also that, according to the voice of the Psalmist, many are the tribulations of the righteous, and the Lord will deliver them from all of these (Ps. 33). Wherefore, dearest sons, we exhort and beseech you to entreat God with frequent prayers, that (St Boniface, ibid.) we and you may be delivered, according to the saying of the Apostle, from troublesome and evil men, for not all have faith (2 Thess. 3). Ask also that our God and Lord, who is the refuge of the poor and the hope of the lowly, may mercifully rescue his holy Church, redeemed namely by his precious blood, and us, who ought to teach, govern, bear and protect that same holy Church, from the aforesaid oppressions and temptations of this wicked world, and from all our necessities, so that the word of God may run (1 Cor. 15) and the glorious Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ may be glorified; and that his grace in us may not become void, lest without the fruit of the Gospel (God forbid!) we appear barren in the sight of God, and return empty of a number of sons and daughters, and be judged guilty of the hidden talent when the Lord comes. For Satan always begrudges these things. And for that reason he stirs up such men against us to press upon us and stifle us, so that he may seize the Lord's sheep without us, and make them fall into the depths, there being no shepherds to guard and defend them. You, therefore, labour with all your strength, and pray and keep watch that these things may not happen, knowing that we are always ready to bring you help in all whatever ways the Lord may give us power, although we ourselves are not exempt from these same rivals of God's holy Church and of ours; and the tribulations of our heart have been greatly enlarged on account of our tribulation and yours, or that of the sheep entrusted to us. We also beseech you not to neglect the service enjoined on you by the Lord, and to strive to help all the oppressed and all the servants of God, and generally all Christians, as the Lord gives you power (St Boniface, letter 26), so that before the tribunal of Christ you may have an everlasting reward. And know that the remembrance of you is constantly before God. For just as we learn with grief that you are troubled by wicked and criminal men, so we continually suffer with you, praying God for the deliverance and relief of your affliction, which (and this distresses us gravely) is inflicted on you day by day by the wicked. And prayers are made for you daily before the bodies of the apostles, that you may be delivered by the Lord's help from troublesome and evil men, and that the sheep entrusted to you may come together with you to the everlasting pastures of eternal life. May almighty God, Creator of all, mindful of us, keep eternally the unity and communion of your Love, strong and advancing for the salvation of all peoples. Amen.
Given on the Nones of April, Valerian and Gallienus, most dear men, being consuls (in the year of Christ 255).
